props.title: They Were Expendable
props.initialSlug: WWII PT boat crews fight against impossible odds

sections.content: John Ford's They Were Expendable stands as one of the most authentic and emotionally resonant WWII films ever made, largely because Ford himself served in the Navy during the war and shot actual combat footage. The film follows PT boat squadrons in the Philippines after Pearl Harbor, with John Wayne and Robert Montgomery (a real PT boat commander) delivering understated performances that avoid the typical war movie bombast. Ford's signature visual style - deep focus photography and carefully composed frames - elevates this beyond standard propaganda, creating a melancholic meditation on sacrifice and duty that influenced later films like The Thin Red Line (1998) and Letters from Iwo Jima (2006).

sections.content: The film marked a crucial transition in how Hollywood depicted WWII, moving from rah-rah patriotism to a more nuanced view of warfare's human cost. While earlier films like Air Force (1943) focused on heroic victories, Ford spotlights the bitter defeat in the Philippines and the psychological toll on soldiers forced to retreat. This influenced later classics like The Bridge on the River Kwai (1957) and Tora! Tora! Tora! (1970) in their unflinching look at the Pacific War's brutal reality.

Ford's documentary experience shaped the film's visual authenticity - he insisted on using real PT boats and actual combat footage when possible. This documentary-drama hybrid approach later influenced films like The Longest Day (1962) and Midway (1976). The scenes of PT boat warfare remain some of the most realistic naval combat ever filmed, achieved through practical effects and Ford's insistence on shooting on location in the Florida Keys. sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond war movies, helping establish the template for the "professional competence" drama where experts face impossible odds. This thread runs through films like The Sand Pebbles (1966) and Master and Commander (2003), which similarly focus on naval leadership under extreme pressure. Ford's emphasis on the camaraderie between sailors and their machines influenced submarine films like Das Boot (1981) and U-571 (2000).
